title: the exit door
hookLine: a boy at Death's door turns down every treasure for one question

cards: A boy named Nachiketa is sitting at the door of Death's house. In the Katha Upanishad, his father, in a burst of temper, has said: I give you to Death. So the boy goes.

Yama, the lord of death, is away, and Nachiketa waits on the doorstep without food for three nights. When Yama comes home, he's embarrassed to have kept a guest waiting, and he offers the boy three wishes.
The first two are easy. The third is a question: what happens to a person after death? Yama tries to talk him out of it.
Ask for something else, he says. Ask for long life, sons and grandsons, cattle, gold, a kingdom. Nachiketa says no.

teach.h: KEEP YOUR HORSES. I WANT TO KNOW.
teach.b: Nachiketa's answer is the heart of today's word. He tells Death that all those treasures wear out, that wealth will never satisfy a person, that even a long life is short. Keep your horses, he says.
I want to know. And Yama, impressed, begins to teach him. That turn, from the list of things to the thing under the list, points straight at today's word.
The tradition speaks of the soul moving through birth after birth, bound by its own actions and desires, and moksha is the knot finally coming untied.

Hindu thought names several aims of a good life: dharma, doing what's yours to do; artha, making a living; kama, love and pleasure. None of those are bad. Moksha sits beyond them, as the freedom the others point toward.
What that freedom is, the schools describe differently.

teach.h: ATMAN IS BRAHMAN, OR LOVE WITH GOD.
teach.b: Advaita Vedanta says it's waking up to what day ten and day eleven already hinted: that atman, the self, is Brahman, and always was.
Devotional schools, such as those centered on Krishna, describe it as living forever in the loving presence of God, never dissolved, never alone.
Some schools teach that a person can be free before death, liberated while still living.
Notice the shape of Nachiketa's choice. He doesn't hate gold. He just won't trade the real question for it.
That's the word in an ordinary day too: the moment you see that the next thing on the list was never going to be enough.

how: In Hindu thought moksha is named alongside dharma, artha and kama as an aim of life, and seekers pursue it through knowledge, devotion, selfless action and meditation, with each school describing liberation in its own way.

games.q: world religions class today. teacher asked what the goal is in Hinduism and i said 'be good, go to heaven?' she said 'not quite' in front of EVERYONE 😩 what's the real answer
o: moksha: release from the cycle of birth after birth. beyond duty, money and pleasure, the freedom they all point toward.
get rich and live a long time.
there's no goal, you just keep being reborn forever.
games.why: Nachiketa turned down Death's gold, cattle and a kingdom to ask the real question. Moksha, release from the cycle of birth after birth, is the aim beyond dharma, artha and kama.

games.q: what's inside the story — tap the pairs.

s: Nachiketa happily takes the treasures Yama offers
he says no. keep your horses; I want to know.
moksha is simply the Hindu word for heaven
it means release: the knot of birth after birth finally untied.
in Hindu thought, wealth and pleasure are aims of life too
artha and kama aren't bad. moksha sits beyond them.

games.q: you're Nachiketa. Death offers you long life, gold, cattle and a kingdom if you'll drop your question about what happens after death. what do you do?
o: take the kingdom. a long life is a good life.
take the gold and ask the question later.
turn it all down and keep the question.
games.why: he turns it all down: the treasures wear out and wealth never satisfies. Yama, impressed, starts to teach him.

practice: Here's the practice: set one thing down. Sit and breathe. Notice one thing you want right now.
A message back, a better week, a number on a screen. Let the wanting be there. Now, just for the length of this sit, set it down beside you.
Not forever. Just: for now, I don't need it. Breathe, and notice what's left when the wanting rests.
If you pray, you can hold that space open to God. The bell holds the time.

wordCard.voice: Moksha. Release. Liberation. The knot untied, the freedom the other aims of life point toward. Nineteenth word.

carryVoice: Your line: freedom is the point. Once today, when you catch yourself chasing the next thing, set it down for one breath, the way Nachiketa set down the gold. Day nineteen.

sources.ref: Katha Upanishad 1.1 (Nachiketa and Yama, the three boons)
